memo.verdict: Bullish; progress to the next stage; conviction medium. Helios Towers (HTWS-GB) is rated a 'Compounder' by pattern with 'Demand Inflection' secondary, B on all four Building Blocks, and the record recommends progression rather than parking. The park rule was applied and not tripped: management B, business quality B, predictability C, trackability C. Conviction is medium rather than high because the framework's metric (brokers'-basis EPS) is the case's weakest line and the two return lenses straddle the 20 percent bar: on the framework's 24-month-forward convention the case clears 20 percent a year up to about 2.85 USD (about 213 pence), on the cash-yield lens only below about 2.62 USD (about 196 pence), and the price of 2.74 USD (205.2 pence, 2026-09-18) sits between them. The record names two conditions under which it would not hold the view: the November 2026 trading update (2026-11-05) showing organic tenancy additions below 600 a quarter, or the FY2026 final dividend not being paid from operating cash. The full Invalidate set: quarterly additions below 600 in Q3 or Q4 2026; FY2027 tenancy guidance below 3,000; unrecognised contract revenue above 55 USDm; the FY2026 final dividend deferred or not funded from operating cash; a convertibility or dividend-repatriation restriction announced in Tanzania or the DRC.
case: Helios Towers is a cash-compounding case with a demand accelerant on top. Its African mobile operators have stepped up network spending, each added tenancy lands on a fixed site cost base, and the balance-sheet repair that kept the cash from shareholders is finished. At 205.2 pence (2.74 USD) the shares pay about 22 percent a year on the framework's convention at an unchanged multiple and about 16 to 17 percent on a cash-yield footing, so the case is compelling on the operating line and merely adequate on the equity line. It turns on whether the tenancy step-up persists into FY2027 and on how much of the EBITDA growth reaches earnings per share.

The change is external, structural and in the customers' own spending. Airtel Africa's cash capex was 389 USDm in the June 2026 quarter against 121 USDm a year earlier; Vodacom raised its medium-term EBITDA and operating free cash flow targets to early-teens growth; the top four African operators raised capex guidance by 33 percent; Orange MEA eCAPEX is tracking to about 1.6 EURbn in 2026. Mobile data in the footprint is forecast to grow twelvefold by 2040 (global sevenfold); Airtel's data usage per customer rose 56 percent; population coverage is 35 percent in the DRC and 45 percent in Tanzania; operators still own about 70 percent of towers in Africa and the Middle East against 31 percent in Europe. That spending produced 1,406 organic tenancy additions in Q1 2026 and 1,105 in Q2 against a consensus of 487, and a second upgrade of FY2026 tenancy guidance to 3,500 to 4,000. The force passes the 'Demand Inflection' test. The caution is that Airtel Africa calls its spending "a deliberate frontloading strategy" and the H2 2026 guidance implies 500 to 750 additions a quarter against 1,255 a quarter in H1, so the step-up may be partly a pull-forward; the record puts it at probable (about two in three) that FY2027 additions are 3,000 or more, the level that confirms the step-change, because the spending is across three operators, the pipeline runs into FY2027, the plan needs only about 1,700 a year, and management has beaten its opening range in each of three years. The other external forces: competition a mild headwind, slowly tightening (Indus Towers licensed in Nigeria, Uganda and Zambia, not Helios markets; SBA building in Tanzania; the Orange DRC and Vodacom joint venture for up to 2,000 solar base stations) but the core intact; disruption a tailwind, the satellite direct-to-cell fear being disproved (Starlink direct-to-cell traffic 0.0003 percent of T-Mobile US usage; terrestrial networks forecast to carry 97 percent of mobile data through 2040); political and regulatory a standing headwind (D) on cost and capital (about 104 USDm of unprovided tax claims; DRC minimum taxes; Tanzanian licensing burdens), unchanged, with Moody's Ba3 upgrade and the Tanzanian central bank's dollar-liquidity support on the other side; supply contained (tower cost stable at 100k to 150k USD; diesel a pass-through); macro a headwind to reported earnings but not to EBITDA (R-squared below 0.05 with currency and Brent since 2015; 71 percent of EBITDA hard currency; a 5 USDm currency drag on Q2 2026 revenue); and one external dynamic on the price alone, the pre-IPO holder exit (Newlight from 8.7 to 4.9 percent; Quantum below 10 percent), which produced a 23 percent pull-back since June 2026.

The internal change is a capital-allocation turn, not a transformation. Four internal forces are strong: guidance raised twice in 2026 and materially (tenancy guidance up 60 percent on the opening range; EBITDA from 515 to 530 USDm to 520 to 535 USDm; recurring free cash flow to 220 to 235 USDm; midpoints raised in each of 2023 to 2025; no red flag); shareholder returns started (inaugural interim dividend 0.604p; 25 USDm FY2026 dividend growing over 10 percent a year; at least 400 USDm through 2030; buyback 58 USDm done under an authorisation raised to 175 USDm to late 2027; not debt-funded); the IMPACT 2030 strategy (organic lease-up over acquisitions; tenancy ratio above 2.5x; over 42,000 tenancies; organic EBITDA CAGR above 9 percent; cumulative recurring free cash flow above 1.3 USDbn; horizon extended to 2040 with 72,000 further addressable tenancies); and rising standards (build time 167 to 102 days; colocation ten days to under 24 hours; uptime 99.99 percent; group ROIC 10.3 percent in 2022 to 14.4 percent in H1 2026). Also the technical defence of terrestrial towers (a white paper of 28 July 2026) as a narrative action against the sector's satellite discount. Absent: chief executive change, perimeter change, new geographies (explicitly deprioritised), new products, real price rises (escalators are nominal and contractual; renewal compression of 20 to 30 percent is the expert's expectation), acquisitions (stepping down: no spend FY2023 to FY2025), balance-sheet utilisation (falling: net debt including leases 1,774 USDm at FY2025 to 1,828 USDm at H1 2026, deleveraging EBITDA-driven). Internal forces B; 'Change Forces' B.
counter_case: At its strongest, as the record carries it: the equity is a leveraged residual on a frontier asset, and the market has just re-rated it on a beat that does not reach it. The tenancy surge is customer front-loading, Airtel Africa's own word for it, and the second-half run rate implied by guidance (500 to 750 a quarter against 1,255 in the first half) already concedes it will roughly halve; Q2 was below Q1. The EBITDA beat is partly power pass-through, 10 USDm of Q2 2026 revenue at nil EBITDA. None of it reaches the shareholder: reported profit fell 30 percent in the half in which Adjusted EBITDA rose 14 percent; consensus FY2026 EPS is down 13 percent in a year and 10.7 percent in three months while every line above it was raised; four brokers disagree by nearly two to one on FY2026 EPS, and the weekly FactSet mean (0.067 USD) is a quarter below the median (0.090 USD) that the record uses as its authority, so the near-term consensus the multiple is applied to is itself too high. The chief executive sold 24 percent of his stake in March 2026 and two pre-IPO holders are still selling; the shares fell 23 percent from June. 46.8 USDm of revenue is unrecognised because customers dispute it, up 149 percent in a year; about 104 USDm of tax claims across three countries are unprovided; the cash reaches London only through Mauritius and central banks that can restrict convertibility, in countries with elevated rule-of-law risk and a regional default precedent (Ghana, December 2022). The moat is contractual rather than economic: the operators are 72 percent of revenue and 90 percent of receivables with no collateral, and at the DRC, Tanzania and Oman renewals from 2027 onward they will take back 20 to 30 percent of the lease rate once the initial capital is amortised, a risk the record itself says it cannot monitor in real time. Meanwhile the equity's claim on the cash sits behind about 2 USDbn of debt and the goodwill of three tax authorities. The multiple has already been re-rated from 13.9x to 17.3x on the 24-month-forward figure, to the 78th percentile of the only history with earnings in it, for a stock the sell-side itself values on cash and EV/EBITDA; European towers are de-rating; the emerging-market towers that are the real comparators trade at 6x EV/EBITDA, about 45 percent below this price, and Morgan Stanley's own bear case is 110p. The whole sell-side is Buy from three or four houses, so there is no one left to upgrade and any downgrade is news. The pattern's own guidance says a correctly modelled, fully discovered high-quality business is a C, not a mis-modelled compounder; the market has learned management's habit of guiding low and prices it in, which is why the July beat-and-raise was not rewarded. Two of the framework's combination red-flag patterns are present on the framework's own metric (a drawdown followed by EPS cuts above 2 percent). Any of three exogenous events (a currency event, a tax ruling, a customer dispute) would expose the equity as the thin, leveraged residual it is, with about 40 to 45 percent of downside to the multiple, and the framework's own drop-through sensitivity shows that two lines management does not control (a 45 percent tax rate and 15 USDm a year more interest) take the eighteen-month return from B to D.

What the record conceded: the EPS fragility and the two red-flag patterns it trips; the front-loading risk until the November update; the P/E re-rating already had; the overhang; the renewal risk, which it cannot monitor in real time; that the downside to 6x EV/EBITDA is about 45 percent; that the pattern's guidance makes "correctly modelled" a C; that the receivables concentration is a structural weakness; and that it cannot refute from the accounts the near-term EPS line being modelled too high. What the record holds against it: the case does not rest on the things conceded; it rests on 5.9 USDbn of non-cancellable contracted revenue with 6.5 years remaining, a 1 percent annual churn cap and all-or-nothing renewal terms that prevent selective decommissioning; a 0.96 correlation between tenancies and Adjusted EBITDA; recurring free cash flow up 52 percent in H1 2026, which pass-through revenue cannot produce; debt fixed at 6.75 percent to 2031 and leverage of 3.4x inside its corridor, which removes the refinancing lever; the Q2 volume miss by consensus being 127 percent rather than a rounding error and the share count demonstrably not in consensus EPS; operator consolidation unlikely in three-to-four-player markets; gross receivables down 12 percent to 157.9 USDm while revenue grew; a former IHS executive's testimony that dollar and CPI linkage are red lines the tower companies have held; and a return that at an unchanged multiple clears the bar on the convention and reaches 16 to 17 percent on cash without any conceded item resolving in the record's favour, plus a distribution programme now running, which a leveraged residual cannot fake for long.
triggers: - Whether the tenancy step-up is structural or front-loaded: the 2026-11-05 Q3 trading update against the implied 500 to 750 a quarter; FY2027 tenancy guidance in March 2027 (3,000 or more confirms the step-change). Alarm: quarterly additions below 750. Invalidate: quarterly additions below 600 in Q3 or Q4 2026, or FY2027 guidance below 3,000. The risks report's annual tripwire: additions below 1,000 a year.

- Whether customer capex persists: Airtel Africa's quarterly cash capex (next print February 2027) and capital intensity; Vodacom's May 2027 results; Orange MEA eCAPEX. Alarm: Airtel Africa quarterly capex below 250 USDm. Invalidate: below 200 USDm a quarter, or capital intensity below 12 percent of revenue.

- Whether the operating growth reaches the equity (the drop-through): the FY2026 reported tax rate (Alarm above 45 percent); a second half in which reported profit falls again while EBITDA rises (the record's own change-of-mind condition); brokers'-basis EPS raised alongside EBITDA at two prints would open the re-rating branch; the sell-side earnings red-flag pattern repeating after the November update would open the de-rating branch. Watch the four brokers' FY2026 EPS dispersion (0.054 to 0.100 USD) and the gap between the FactSet mean and median.

- Whether the cash can leave the countries: the FY2026 final dividend (March 2027) paid from operating cash; central bank convertibility policy in Tanzania and the DRC; dividends paid to equity holders against cash generated. Invalidate: a convertibility or dividend-repatriation restriction announced in either country, or dividends paid to equity holders below 15 USDm in a year of cash generation above 550 USDm. Alarm: a new material tax assessment or a sovereign downgrade in the DRC or Tanzania.

- Whether the distribution programme holds: net leverage reaching about 3.0x by end-FY2026; buyback execution under the 175 USDm programme; the possible lowering of the corridor or a step-up toward the 800 USDm Deutsche Bank models. Alarm: the buyback paused or leverage above 3.5x. Invalidate: the FY2026 final dividend deferred or not funded from operating cash.

- Lease-renewal pricing in the DRC, Tanzania and Oman from 2027: not monitorable in real time; Alarm on any renewal disclosed at a materially lower lease rate; the expert expectation is 20 to 30 percent compression.
